This module cites no AABB Standards text — QSE (Quality System Essential) 4 is named and
themed only, the same handling this curriculum gives every AABB Standard. The links below
are AABB's own public pages describing the framework this module's tiering scheme sits
under, plus the internal-course link back to the incident this module's running example
reuses, a video, and several outside references on supplier and supply-chain risk. All were checked and loading at the time this page was written.

- **[AABB: Updated Quality Systems Essentials](https://www.aabb.org/standards-accreditation/standards/about-aabb-standards/updated-quality-systems-essentials)**
  — AABB's own public page confirming the ten-element Quality System Essentials structure
  (QSE 4 is "Supplier and Customer Issues," the element this module applies) and that all
  current AABB Standards are built on this template. Read it for the structure, not a
  specific standard number — this page doesn't enumerate the ten element titles itself.

- **[AABB: Proposed 34th Edition of *Standards for Blood Banks and Transfusion
  Services*](https://www.aabb.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/standards/proposed-34th-edition-of-standards-for-blood-banks-and-transfusion-services.pdf?sfvrsn=8d0d4f7b_0)**
  (PDF) — a proposed, comment-period edition, not confirmed as currently adopted text, but
  the clearest publicly available document naming all ten QSE-aligned chapters, including
  "Suppliers and Customers." Useful if you want to see the supplier-and-customer element
  named inside an actual (proposed) Standards document, rather than taking this lesson's
  paraphrase on faith. Do not cite a chapter or standard number from this PDF as current,
  adopted AABB text — it's a comment-period draft.

- **[Investigating a Healthcare Data Incident](../../healthcare-security-and-privacy/investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident/index.qmd)**
  — the final module of `healthcare-security-and-privacy`, where the device-management
  platform vendor, the Brookfield laptop, and the permanently unresolved encryption
  question were all first established. Read it (or re-read it) before module 2 — this
  course's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 modules assume you remember exactly what that investigation
  did and didn't resolve.

- **[Risk-Based Vendor Due Diligence: Identifying the Proper Scope, Scale, and Documents Webinar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e4wBnhqiS14)**
  (Venminder, from oEmbed `author_name`) — the video embedded in this lesson. A third-party
  risk management company's training on matching due-diligence depth to a vendor's risk. It is
  general industry training, not blood- or FDA-specific. Verified embeddable via YouTube oEmbed
  on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/161/r1/final)**
  — NIST's publication page for its supply-chain risk guidance, covering how organizations manage
  risk from their suppliers and the systems and services they depend on. Read it for a government-grade version of
  the same "how much scrutiny does this supplier earn" reasoning; it is not an AABB or FDA
  requirement. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[FDA: Contract Manufacturing Arrangements for Drugs: Quality Agreements Guidance for Industry](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/contract-manufacturing-arrangements-drugs-quality-agreements)**
  — FDA's own guidance page on written quality agreements between a manufacturer and its
  suppliers or contractors. It is drug-focused, not blood-specific, but it is the clearest FDA
  explanation of what a written quality agreement is for, the document the Medium tier in this
  lesson relies on "where relevant." Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 606.65, Supplies and reagents](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/606.65)**
  — the blood-establishment regulation on the supplies and reagents used in collection, testing
  and processing. Read it to see the federal text behind why a reagent supplier with no data
  access still bears on a regulated process. It is not quoted or cited in the lesson itself, so
  read the current text there rather than relying on this summary. Verified loading
  via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 211.84, Testing and approval or rejection of components, drug product containers, and closures](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/211.84)**
  — a drug-GMP counterpart showing how a regulated manufacturer is expected to qualify and
  verify what its suppliers deliver. It applies to finished-drug manufacturers, not blood
  establishments, so use it as a comparison point only. Verified loading via `curl` on
  2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

## Keep learning

Not official sources — good places to learn more about vendor qualification and risk tiering.

- **[Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM): Concepts and Mitigations](https://destcert.com/resources/supply-chain-risk-management/)** (Destination Certification) — CISSP study guide page on supply chain risk, including third-party assessment, minimum requirements and monitoring; supports CISSP Domain 1 (Security and Risk Management). Commercial training site. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[Certified: The CISSP Audio Course, Episode 100: Assessing Third-Party and Vendor Risk](https://share.transistor.fm/s/58b9f28c)** (Certified: The CISSP Audio Course podcast) — a short listen on why vendor relationships add risk and how to assess it; good commuting reinforcement for CISSP Domain 1. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[Third-Party Assurance: Why and How?](https://www.isaca.org/resources/isaca-journal/issues/2021/volume-2/third-party-assurance)** (ISACA Journal, 2021) — ranks the kinds of vendor evidence from self-assessment to independent reports, a useful lens when deciding how much proof each Lakeshore tier deserves. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[Information Sharing in Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management – A New Model](https://www.isc2.org/insights/2024/06/information-sharing-in-cyber-supply-chain-risk-management-a-new-model)** (ISC2 Insights) — a practitioner-body view of why supply chain risk can't be managed vendor by vendor in isolation; background for CISSP Domain 1. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[Third-Party Risk Management for Healthcare: The 2026 HIPAA Guide](https://medcurity.com/third-party-risk-management-healthcare/)** (Medcurity — vendor/commercial content) — a healthcare-focused walk through inventorying, tiering and reviewing vendors; helpful HCISPP-style context. Treat as marketing-adjacent, not as authority. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
